entry.title: Arias v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1903
entry.content:
This case concerned two out-of-time judicial review applications by a Colombian citizen challenging ART decisions affirming the cancellation of his Bridging C (Subclass 030) visa and the refusal of his Partner (Temporary) (Subclass 820) visa. The Court refused both extensions of time because the proposed grounds had no reasonable prospects of success and ordered costs in each matter.

Key holding: Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time should be refused where the proposed grounds of judicial review have no prospects of success.

Where there are no prospects of the applicant's grounds of review succeeding, an extension is to be refused.

entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2505
entry.content:
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Secretary, Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure v Thaler (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 226
entry.content:
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. It otherwise dismissed the motion, with no order as to the costs of the motion.

Key holding: The Court of Appeal may, under cl 29(8)(d) of Sch 5 to the NCAT Act, direct NCAT to determine remitted costs without requiring special circumstances under s 60.

The power extends to authorising the Tribunal to depart from the rule in s 60 (which rule is explicitly displaced in a number of places in the Act: see Schedule 3 cll 12 and 13 and Schedule 5 cll 23 and 26, and Civil and Administrative Tribunal Rules 2014, rr 38 and 38A).

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: SRQY and Child Support Registrar (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2480
entry.content:
The Tribunal dealt with a child support care percentage dispute after two boys commenced boarding school and a maternal grandfather paid the school fees. It set aside the first review decision and restored the existing 50%/50% care percentage determinations. The Tribunal held that, on the evidence, the actual care taking place still corresponded with the existing care percentages.

Key holding: Where the actual care that is taking place corresponds with the existing care percentage, the care percentage determination cannot be revoked under ss 54F or 54H of the Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989.

It further follows that the care that was actually taking place corresponded with the existing care percentage. In these circumstances, the child support law does not permit the existing care percentage determination to be revoked.

entry.title: Testart v Testart (No 3) [2026] FCA 1558
entry.content:
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.

Key holding: A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

entry.title: Riddell v State of Queensland (Department of Education) [2026] QIRC 338
entry.content:
The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission allowed Ms Riddell’s public service appeal against a refusal to convert her temporary HP3 Occupational Therapist employment to permanent. The Commission held the refusal was not fair and reasonable because the decision-maker confined the substantially-same-role inquiry to vacant positions, gave inadequate reasons, and treated backfilling/no vacancy as a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion.

Key holding: The absence of a vacant permanent position does not, of itself, amount to a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion of temporary employment to permanent; the decision-maker must focus on the role or a substantially same role.

As has been noted in numerous decisions from the Commission, some of which have been cited above, the lack of a vacant permanent position is not a genuine operational requirement or impediment to the Appellant's temporary employment being converted to permanent. It is expected in this scenario that a position will be created.

entry.title: BDCN and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2432
entry.content:
This was a second review of child support care percentages for two children. The Father alleged the Mother ceased providing care from January 2024 when the family lost its home, with older daughters and friends said to be providing care. The Tribunal found the Mother continued to arrange and provide care, including delegated care, and affirmed the existing 100% care determination to her.

Key holding: A parent’s percentage of care is not reduced merely because care is temporarily delivered through others or because older children assist, where the parent continues to arrange, financially support and meet the children’s needs.

Taking all of the above matters into account, I am not satisfied that the care of the children actually taking place no longer corresponded with the existing percentage of care determination of 100% to the Mother for each of the 2 children.

entry.title: Hormaza v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1925
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of an ART decision affirming refusal of a student visa for failing to meet English language proficiency requirements. He alleged procedural unfairness, his migration agent’s negligence, legal unreasonableness, and the ART’s use of the wrong legislative instrument. The Court dismissed the application, finding no jurisdictional error and that the instrument error was immaterial.

Key holding: A representative’s negligence or administrative error in failing to notify an applicant of a hearing does not, without fraud or dishonesty, vitiate the Tribunal’s decision.

As stated in DUA16 at [15], "an administrative decision [under the Act] is not vitiated merely by bad or negligent advice or some other mishap that leads to detriment to an applicant", including negligence by a representative.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Martin v Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW) [2026] NSWSC 1288
entry.content:
This was a NSW Supreme Court appeal against Local Court convictions for a sexual act towards a child and attempted voyeurism. Hamill J allowed the appeal because the Acting Magistrate’s ex tempore reasons were inadequate and failed to address the onus and standard of proof and key exculpatory evidence and submissions. The DPP conceded error.

Key holding: A conviction will be vitiated by an error of law where the judicial officer’s reasons fail to disclose the onus and standard of proof applied and fail to explain why exculpatory evidence and submissions were rejected.

The failure to provide adequate reasons - including but not limited to, the failure to mention the requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt - amounted to a fundamental failure of process and amounted to a clear error of law.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: WNZP and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2398
entry.content:
This was a second review in a child support matter concerning the parents’ percentage of care for two children after the Mother notified a change of care on 23 March 2024. The Tribunal recalculated actual care, rejected an argument that the Father’s overseas absences meant he had relinquished care, and declined to record court-ordered care under s 51 because the change predated 29 March 2024. The decision under review was set aside and new care percentages were substituted.

Key holding: Under the law applying before 29 March 2024, an interim care determination under s 51 cannot be made where existing care percentages are revoked under s 54F or s 54H.

I am bound by the Court's interpretation in CMU23 and must apply the legislation in force prior to 29 March 2024, specifically paragraph 53(1)(c), such that an interim determination cannot be made when existing percentages of care are revoked either pursuant to section 54F or section 54H of the Act.

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: South Australian Commission for Catholic Schools Inc and Secretary, Department of Education (Guidance and Appeals Panel) [2026] ARTA 2304
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed 2024 Commonwealth recurrent funding determinations for 84 non-government Catholic schools in South Australia. It unanimously held that mid-year reception students who began in term 3 2024 were “primary students” because reception was the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1. A majority then held those students did not have a pattern of regular attendance at school or school generally during 2024, so they failed reg 9B(1)(c) and were ineligible unless the Minister included them under reg 9B(3).

Key holding: Reception undertaken by mid-year reception students is the “foundation” year of schooling immediately before year 1, so those students are primary students in that calendar year.

Giving the phrases to which I have already referred their natural meaning, the logical conclusion is that the 2024 mid-year reception students were in the year of schooling in a course of primary education that was immediately before year 1. It follows that, in 2024, those students were in the foundation year of schooling, were receiving primary education and were therefore primary students at their school.

entry.title: Tran and Australian Skills Quality Authority [2026] ARTA 2300
entry.content:

Although the Tribunal found the s 56(1)(a) ground was established because Kingsway did not provide or arrange the necessary assessment, it exercised the discretion not to cancel in exceptional circumstances. The Tribunal is satisfied that the discretion under subsection 56(1) of the NVR Act not to cancel the Qualification can be safely and appropriately exercised in the exceptional circumstances of this case. That discretion may be exercised consistent with the public interest, given that Mr Tran possesses the requisite training, skills and work experience to have been awarded the Qualification on an RPL basis.

entry.title: OZY25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FedCFamC2G 1983
entry.content:
The applicants sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of Subclass 866 protection visas. They alleged jurisdictional error arising from their former representative’s conduct, which they said caused an uninformed request for a decision on the papers and stultified the statutory review process. The Federal Circuit and Family Court dismissed the application, finding the factual foundation for the alleged stultification was not proved.

Key holding: A claim that representative conduct affected the validity of a Tribunal decision requires proof of the alleged failure and its disabling effect; it cannot be inferred merely from hindsight that a hearing might have offered forensic advantages.

Whatever duties s 56 may impose upon a representative, a failure capable of affecting the validity of the Tribunal's decision must first be proved. Section 56 does not permit the Court to infer deficient advice merely from the fact that, with hindsight, attendance might have offered additional forensic opportunities.

He argued the Tribunal failed to consider his study evidence and possible exemptions in IMMI 18/015, and relied on COVID-19 and mistaken agent advice.

Key holding: Where an exemption is plainly not engaged on the materials, a tribunal’s minimal engagement with documentary evidence can be within the bounds of rationality and reasonableness, so no jurisdictional error is shown.

The degree of effort needed by the decision maker to engage with the evidence about the Diploma and Advanced Diploma was minimal in circumstances where it was obvious that clause 6(2)(d)(i) and (ii) of the Instrument were not engaged. In the circumstances of the case, I am satisfied that the extent of the Tribunal's engagement with the documentary evidence occurred within the bounds of rationality and reasonableness and no jurisdictional error is demonstrated.

entry.content:

Although she failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke the cancellation. The decision under review was set aside and the visa cancellation revoked under s 501CA(4).

Key holding: Where a non-citizen fails the character test after mandatory visa cancellation, the Tribunal may revoke cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) if satisfied there is another reason, exercising the discretion in accordance with the applicable ministerial direction.

Section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act requires the Tribunal to consider if there is another reason why the discretion should be exercised to revoke the original decision. In exercising this discretion, the Tribunal must have regard to the Direction (s 499(2A)).

entry.title: Majak and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2277
entry.content:
Majak sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class XB Subclass 202 visa under s 501(3A) after serious assault convictions. The Tribunal accepted he failed the character test but found “another reason” to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), principally the best interests of his infant daughter and the extreme impediments if removed to South Sudan. It set aside the delegate’s decision and substituted revocation.

Key holding: Where the Tribunal is satisfied on the evidence that another reason exists, it should set aside the non-revocation decision and substitute revocation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Having reached this conclusion, I find that there is 'another reason' for the revocation of the cancellation decision for the purposes of section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act. Accordingly, it is appropriate for me to set aside the decision under review and substitute decision that the cancellation decision be revoked.

entry.title: FPXJ and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2321
entry.content:
The Applicant, FPXJ, sought an extension of time to bring second review applications in the Administrative Review Tribunal against two AAT first review decisions dated 19 August 2019 and 29 January 2020 concerning disability support pension debts. The Tribunal rejected his procedural and bias arguments and refused the extension. It found the delay exceeded six years, was not fully explained, and that reopening settled matters would prejudice the Respondent and wider public, with no practical utility in the substantive review.

Key holding: Under s 19 of the ART Act, the Tribunal may refuse an extension of time where significant delay, prejudice and lack of practical utility mean it is not reasonable in all the circumstances to extend time.

Given this, and given the prejudice to the Respondent and to the wider public if an extension of time is granted, the Tribunal has decided that it is not reasonable in all of the circumstances to extend time for the Applicant to make second review applications. The extension of time applications are refused by the Tribunal.
